samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a concrete single-source plan with version-tagged differences. B wins mainly because it assigns chapter ownership to the two writers, which A never does, and it says to fix and log drift while diffing before retiring and redirecting the old copies. A gives stronger tooling detail and a staged rollout by priority, but it fills the plan with invented effort figures and builds out more CI and tooling than two writers need. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B gives the more concrete single-source mechanics, with drift buckets, conditionals, separate per-version files for big differences, and a cutover diff, but it never says which of the two writers owns what. A splits ownership between Writer 1 and Writer 2 and adds a fix-checked-across-versions rule, though it drifts into extras like an engineering definition of done and monthly reviews. Both make up time figures and lean toward a full migration rather than starting with the most-fixed pages.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a solid plan to merge into a single source with version markers. A explicitly sorts drift from real version differences, gives section ownership to the two writers and declines to invent estimates. B is technically richer, but it makes up figures (day and week durations, 'about five conditionals', 'large majority') and leans toward a full migration with CI and PR tooling, while only lightly covering ownership. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers propose a single source with version markers. B handles ownership better, starts with a staged pilot chapter, deals with drift by taking the newest correct text, and refuses to estimate without seeing the guides. A gives a solid technical plan but invents figures (day and week estimates, a budget of five conditionals, 'the large majority' of pages) and turns the fix into a full migration with CI, while B adds some extra process (freshness dates, feedback replies) but stays small enough for two people.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers propose one shared source built into three outputs. A leans on a heavier CI and tooling migration and includes made-up figures ('2–3 weeks part-time', 'ten seconds'), while B adds a few extra roles (a release owner and support or engineering staff) beyond the two writers. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a concrete single-source plan. A sorts sections more clearly into same, intended and accidental differences, adds a fix log for the period before the merge, and stays with the writers' existing tools, though it invents a support/engineering verifier and a release owner. B adds new tooling and CI, which is a lot of process for two writers, and it invents figures such as '2–3 weeks part-time' and 'ten seconds'.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A deals best with the main problem. It names a backup reviewer, sets a time limit with escalation and makes the release wait instead of shipping without a check, though its sample day counts are only labeled as defaults in a note at the end. B uses clear placeholders and splits steps that must be run from a read-through where silence counts as approval, but it names no fallback for the person who runs the steps and lets an unchecked guide ship with a banner. Neither answer uses role terms like the engineer who owns that component, and A does not say which small wording fixes may skip full review. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a rule you can paste into a wiki and both require running the steps. A leaves names and deadlines as placeholders, separates the read-through from the run-through, and provides a fallback (wait or ship with an 'unverified' banner). It doesn't name who runs the steps by role, though, and it doesn't spell out which small edits can skip review. B handles the reviewer who never answers better, with a backup reviewer and escalation. But it states 3/2/1 business days as if they were settled facts and only calls them defaults at the end. It also lacks a proportionality tier, so even small wording fixes need a full run-through.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is better. It treats wording, typo and formatting fixes differently from changes to steps, commands and versions, and it leaves names, time limits and channels as clear placeholders. A puts fixed day counts in the rule itself and never says which small edits can ship without a full review, though its requirement to run every step on a clean machine is strong. Both handle a reviewer who never answers well, but B's options to hold the changed steps or publish with a banner are more practical than A's override approach. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A is the better answer because it handles proportionality and placeholders better. It separates wording, typo and formatting fixes, which need only the owner's okay, from changed steps, commands and versions, which need a recorded run-through, and it leaves every name, time limit and channel as a clearly marked placeholder. B has a stronger testing requirement (a clean machine and a reviewer who can run the product) and a solid escalation path, but it treats every edit the same and puts specific day counts (3, 1 and 2 days, plus a 1-day fix target) into the rule text, mentioning only in a note that they can be changed.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a rule you could paste into a wiki and require that the steps be run, not just read. A uses placeholders for every number and name, and makes the rule proportionate with its risk-based silence handling and urgent short path. B handles the silent reviewer best, with a backup reviewer, escalation times and the manager as the final step, but it states its timings as facts in the rule text and never says what may ship with lighter review. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a rule that could be pasted into a wiki and require the steps to be run, not just read. A deals with a silent reviewer more cleanly, with a named backup and a clear rule that the guide doesn't publish once the deadline passes. B uses clear placeholders instead of fixed day counts, ties guide updates to product changes, and offers a proportionate short path by step type, though it has no backup reviewer. Neither answer clearly separates small wording fixes from changed steps, and B wins narrowly on proportionality and on not presenting numbers as facts.
